item.title: JADEPUFFER Langflow RCE, FortiBleed Ransomware Access, and ChocoPoC Fake PoCs
item.content:encoded:
AI Agent Exploits Langflow RCE to Automate Database Ransomware Attack — Must Read

Sysdig says JADEPUFFER used an AI agent to autonomously exploit an unpatched Langflow RCE, steal credentials, pivot into MySQL/Nacos, and destroy a production database with a ransom note. The key lesson is that exposed, unpatched AI and infrastructure tools with stored secrets can now be chained into full ransomware-style attacks at machine speed.

  • Sysdig says it found what it believes is the first ransomware attack run from start to finish by an AI agent, tracked as JADEPUFFER.
  • JADEPUFFER exploited CVE-2025-3248, an already-patched missing-authentication flaw in Langflow that allows unauthenticated Python code execution on reachable servers.
  • After gaining access, the agent searched for secrets, accessed a MinIO server using the default minioadmin:minioadmin credentials, and created a scheduled task that contacted the attacker’s server every 30 minutes.
  • The agent pivoted to an internet-facing MySQL and Nacos server, logged into the database as root, abused CVE-2021-29441 and a default Nacos signing key, and created its own admin account.
  • The agent encrypted 1,342 Nacos settings, dropped the original tables, deleted whole databases, and left a ransom note, but the encryption key was printed once and not saved or sent anywhere.

FortiBleed Credential Theft Linked to INC and Lynx Ransomware Operations — Must Read

SOCRadar linked the FortiBleed FortiGate credential-theft campaign to INC and Lynx ransomware operations, showing stolen admin access was used for follow-on ransomware intrusions. The campaign scanned thousands of FortiGate portals globally, confirmed access to hundreds of targets, and has already led to at least 12 ransomware deployments.

  • SOCRadar attributed the FortiBleed credential-theft campaign to INC and Lynx ransomware operations after finding an operator tied to FortiBleed infrastructure actively working negotiation panels for both groups.
  • SOCRadar tracked scanning activity against about 11,250 FortiGate portals in more than 150 countries, confirmed admin-level access on 409 targets, and said the full attack chain was completed on 354 of them.
  • At least 12 ransomware deployments have resulted from the access, encrypting hundreds of endpoints across affected organizations.
  • The FortiBleed operation involved scanning exposed Fortinet devices, using known credential combinations to access them, and deploying custom packet sniffers to collect credentials and authentication data from network traffic.
  • SOCRadar said tooling, logs, and working hours point to a Russian-speaking threat actor likely operating as an initial access broker, with much of the targeting focused on manufacturing, technology, and logistics sectors in Latin America and the Asia Pacific regions.

New ChocoPoC RAT Targets Vulnerability Researchers via Fake PoC Exploit Repos — Should Read

Attackers are targeting vulnerability researchers with fake GitHub PoC exploit repos that hide the ChocoPoC data-stealing RAT inside Python dependencies. Researchers should treat unverified PoCs and their dependency chains as hostile, and anyone who installed packages like frint or skytext should rotate credentials and rebuild affected systems.

  • Attackers are distributing the ChocoPoC remote access trojan through fake Python proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub that claim to exploit newly public CVEs.
  • The visible proof-of-concept code appears clean because the malware is hidden in Python dependencies, including frint and skytext, with skytext carrying compiled files named gradient.so on Linux and gradient.pyd on Windows.
  • ChocoPoC can steal saved passwords, browser cookies, autofill data, browsing history, text files, notes, local databases, shell history, network settings, and process lists, and it can run shell commands or arbitrary Python.
  • YesWeHack and Sekoia found at least seven fake proof-of-concept repositories tied to high-profile flaws, and the skytext package had been downloaded about 2,400 times, mostly on Linux.
  • The article advises researchers to treat proof-of-concept code as hostile, inspect the full dependency chain, avoid code from new or unknown accounts, and check systems for frint, skytext, slogsec, and logcrypt.cryptography.

Alleged Scattered Spider hacker extradited to the United States — Should Read

A 19-year-old dual U.S.-Estonian citizen accused of being part of the Scattered Spider hacking group has been extradited to the United States to face fraud, conspiracy, and computer intrusion charges. Prosecutors say the group has carried out more than 100 intrusions and caused over $100 million in ransom payments.

  • Peter Stokes, a 19-year-old dual U.S. and Estonian citizen, was extradited to the United States to face charges alleging he was a member of the Scattered Spider hacking collective.
  • Stokes was arrested in Finland on April 10 while attempting to board a flight to Japan at Helsinki's airport.
  • Court documents allege Stokes was involved in at least four Scattered Spider breaches, including a March 2023 hack of an online communication platform and a May 2025 breach of a multibillion-dollar luxury item retailer.
  • In the luxury retailer case, hackers allegedly used calls to the company’s IT helpdesk while posing as employees to reset credentials and access administrator accounts, then demanded an $8 million ransom.
  • U.S. officials said Scattered Spider has been involved in over 100 network intrusions that resulted in more than $100 million in ransom payments and millions more in damages to victims.

Missed incidents, persistent threats, and response gaps: Insights from compromise assessment projects — May Read

Kaspersky’s 2025 compromise assessments found that many organizations miss serious intrusions for months or years because security tools are poorly monitored, tuned, or supported by threat hunting. Regular proactive assessments, continuous monitoring, better asset and vulnerability management, and practiced incident response are key to finding hidden persistence before it becomes high-severity compromise.

  • Kaspersky’s 2025 compromise assessment engagements found that 30.8% of incidents had activity spanning more than three months, and 52% of high-severity compromises were discovered only after 90 days of going undetected.
  • Organizations that requested compromise assessments after a cybersecurity incident had the highest share of high-severity findings at 40.7%, while organizations conducting regular audits had the lowest share of high-severity issues at 27.7%.
  • Kaspersky reported that 60% of discovered incidents were missed because existing tools did not generate high-confidence alerts, while 20% of incidents were found manually.
  • The report found that 40% of discovered web shells were stored in backups, creating a risk that restoring backups could reintroduce malicious files after incident response activities.
  • Remote management tools and living-off-the-land binaries were observed in every compromise assessment engagement that resulted in incident detection.

The AI Dilemma in Healthcare: Innovating Without Risking Security — Optional

Healthcare organizations are rapidly adopting AI, but widespread shadow AI and legacy infrastructure are creating serious risks to patient data, compliance, and security. The key takeaway is that AI innovation in healthcare needs strong governance through modern zero trust and SASE architectures to be safe.

  • Netskope’s survey of North American healthcare IT leaders found that 67% of healthcare organizations are building their own AI applications, while 52% have approved standalone AI apps and are integrating AI into existing SaaS platforms.
  • Half of healthcare organizations report using AI without corporate oversight, creating shadow AI risks when staff input sensitive patient data into unmanaged large language models.
  • Healthcare leaders cited legacy infrastructure and technical debt as barriers, with 49% saying current infrastructure slows new AI initiatives and 28% saying legacy systems actively hold back innovation.
  • The article says traditional perimeter-based security is insufficient for AI use in healthcare because data moves between clinicians, cloud apps, and third-party models.
  • Healthcare leaders using zero trust and secure access service edge architectures reported benefits including better network performance, faster launches of new products and services, and operational efficiency and cost reduction.
